exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator

question.explanation:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form: \begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 4} \dfrac {\sqrt{2x -7} -1} {x-4}&= \dfrac {\sqrt{2(4) -7} -1} {4-4}=\dfrac{0}{0} \end{align*}

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

\[ \eqalign{ \lim_{x \to 4} \dfrac {\sqrt{2x - 7} - 1} {x - 4}&=\lim_{x \to 4} \dfrac {(\sqrt{2x - 7} - 1)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)} {(x - 4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)}\\[5pt] &=\lim_{x \to 4} \dfrac {\left(\sqrt{2x - 7}\right)^2 - 1^2} {(x - 4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)}\\[5pt] &=\lim_{x \to 4} \dfrac {2x - 7- 1} {(x - 4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)}\\[5pt] &=\lim_{x \to 4} \dfrac {2x - 8} {(x - 4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)}\\[5pt] &=\lim_{x \to 4} \dfrac {2(x - 4)} {(x - 4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)}\\[5pt] &=\lim_{x \to 4} \dfrac {2} {\sqrt{2x-7}+1}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac {2} {\sqrt{2(4)-7}+1}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac {2}{1+1}\\[5pt] &=1. } \]

example.title: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator

question.explanation:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form: \begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3^-} \dfrac {3-\sqrt{3x}} {x-3}&= \dfrac {3-\sqrt{3(3)}} {3-3}=\dfrac{0}{0} \end{align*}

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get \begin{align} \lim_{x \to 3^-} \dfrac {3 - \sqrt{3x}} {x - 3} &= \lim_{x \to 3^-} \dfrac {\left(3 - \sqrt{3x}\right)\left(3+\sqrt {3x}\right)}{(x - 3)\left(3+\sqrt {3x}\right)} \\[5pt] &= \lim_{x \to 3^-} \dfrac {3^2-\left(\sqrt{3x}\right)^2}{(x - 3)\left(3+\sqrt {3x}\right)} \\[5pt] &= \lim_{x \to 3^-} \dfrac {9-3x}{(x - 3)\left(3+\sqrt {3x}\right)} \\[5pt] &= \lim_{x \to 3^-} \dfrac {-3(x-3)}{(x - 3)\left(3+\sqrt {3x}\right)} \\[5pt] &= \lim_{x \to 3^-} \dfrac {-3}{3+\sqrt {3x}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {-3}{3+\sqrt {3\cdot 3}} \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac 1 2. \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator

question.explanation:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=0$, we get an indeterminate form: \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{x \to 3} \dfrac {x^{2} - 9} {\sqrt{x+1} - 2} &= \dfrac {3^{2} - 9} {\sqrt{3+1} - 2} =\dfrac{0}{0} \end{align*}

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get \begin{align} \lim\limits_{x \to 3} \dfrac {x^{2} - 9} {\sqrt{x+1} - 2} &=\lim\limits_{x \to 3} \dfrac{\big(x^{2} - 9\big)\big(\sqrt{x+1} + 2\big)} {\big(\sqrt{x+1} - 2\big)\big(\sqrt{x+1} + 2\big)} \\[5pt] &=\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3} \dfrac{(x-3)(x+3)\big(\sqrt{x+1} + 2\big)}{\big(\sqrt{x+1}\big)^{2} - 2^2} \\[5pt] &=\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3} \dfrac{(x-3)(x+3)\big(\sqrt{x+1} + 2\big)}{(x+1)-4} \\[5pt] &=\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3} \dfrac{(x-3)(x+3)\big(\sqrt{x+1} + 2\big)}{x-3} \\[5pt] &=\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3} \dfrac{\cancel{(x-3)}(x+3)\big(\sqrt{x+1} + 2\big)}{\cancel{x-3}} \\[5pt] &=\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3} \: (x+3)\big(\sqrt{x+1} + 2\big) \\[5pt] &= (3+3)\big(\sqrt{3+1} + 2\big) \\[5pt] &= 6(4)\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{24}. \end{align}

example.title: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator

question.explanation:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=8$, we get an indeterminate form: \begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 8^+} \dfrac {x - 8}{4 - \sqrt{2x}} &= \dfrac {8 - 8}{4 - \sqrt{2\cdot 8}} =\dfrac{0}{0} \end{align*}

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

\[ \eqalign{ \lim_{x \to 8^+} \dfrac {x - 8}{4 - \sqrt{2x}} &= \lim_{x \to 8^+} \dfrac {(x - 8)\left(4+\sqrt {2x}\right)}{\left(4 - \sqrt{2x}\right)\left(4+\sqrt {2x}\right)} \\[5pt] &= \lim_{x \to 8^+} \dfrac {(x - 8)(4+\sqrt {2x})}{4^2-\left(\sqrt{2x}\right)^2} \\[5pt] &= \lim_{x \to 8^+} \dfrac {(x - 8)(4+\sqrt {2x})}{16-2x} \\[5pt] &= \lim_{x \to 8^+} \dfrac {(x - 8)(4+\sqrt {2x})}{-2(x-8)} \\[5pt] &= \lim_{x \to 8^+} \dfrac {4+\sqrt {2x}}{-2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {4+\sqrt {2(8)}}{-2} \\[5pt] &=-4. } \]

example.title: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator

question.explanation:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=4$, we get an indeterminate form: \begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 4^+} \dfrac {x - 4}{\sqrt{3x - 3} - 3}&= \dfrac {4 - 4}{\sqrt{3(4) - 3} - 3}=\dfrac{0}{0} \end{align*}

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

\[ \eqalign{ \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x - 4}{\sqrt{3x - 3} - 3}&=\lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {(x - 4)(\sqrt{3x-3}+3)}{(\sqrt{3x - 3} - 3)(\sqrt{3x-3}+3)}\\[5pt] &=\lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {(x - 4)(\sqrt{3x-3}+3)}{\left(\sqrt{3x - 3}\right)^2 - 3^2}\\[5pt] &=\lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {(x - 4)(\sqrt{3x-3}+3)}{3x - 3- 9}\\[5pt] &=\lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {(x - 4)(\sqrt{3x-3}+3)}{3x - 12}\\[5pt] &=\lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {(x - 4)(\sqrt{3x-3}+3)}{3(x - 4)}\\[5pt] &=\lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {\sqrt{3x-3}+3}{3}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac {\sqrt{3(4)-3}+3}{3}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac {3+3}{3}\\[5pt] &=2. } \]
